t: Can Ten Minutes of Reading Change a Whole Semester of Teaching? It May Have for This Teacher
q: It completely changed my perspective, re-oriented me to why I am doing what I am doing, reminded me of the point of education, helped me pare down my self-demands, and allowed me to enjoy my first class. Not bad for 6 pages.
The gist is that a small bit of reading — just six pages — significantly shifted what Nora was believing about teaching as she approached her first day.
In other words, a very small intervention — six pages of words, from one colleague to another — achieved an inner shift that disrupted the workload-pressure doom loop.

Workload goes up — There is an insurmountable number of things that we teachers feel or are told that we are responsible for doing. Pressure goes up — There is inevitably a portion of this un-complete-able responsibilities list that we feel inadequate to handle — it's outside of our competency areas.
In other words, Nora's experience of pressure in her work decreased, her performance likely increased, and her enjoyment of the whole deal increased as well. That's what we call a win-win-win.

t: Steady Goes It: It's Tortoise Time
q: But look: you and I are in the business of making long-term plans. It's never all or nothing for us. It's "Today, I'm going to get a bit better at this one thing. Tomorrow, I'll keep on that path. Bit by bit, I will progress toward expertise.
Is there a better investment in ourselves than the pursuit of expertise — of a ready knowledgeability about our work, a time-steadied gaze at the work that matters most? I don't think so.
COVID taught us a lot about the Workload-Pressure Paradox and the Journey of the Teacher's Heart. I want to spend a few weeks on practical considerations.

A lot of folks are going to drive themselves crazy this month using hare-like intensity to enter the school year on the brink of burnout. Not you and me. We know that we'll always be learning — and we're okay with that.
Focus on the work that matters most. Competence grows one day at a time; focus is its best accelerator.
Master the material. That's the mantra I've been using with my students the past few years. Mastery is fun, rewarding, communal, sweet.

t: My Own Secret Strategy For The First Day Of School
q: The strategy, which takes just a few seconds, sends a powerful message to your new students. It gets to the quick, ending any doubt about whether you’re a teacher who will do what you say you will.
It’s a bit sneaky and may need adjusting according to your grade level, but it effectively eliminates the testing phase whereby students push and probe to find the limits of your patience.
For elementary students I recommend asking them to stay silent while you’re talking. This can also work for middle school.
So for high-schoolers I recommend asking them to keep their phones out of sight and letting them know that you’ll take them away if you see them.
Now, it’s important that you do this after a long pause, and be sure to take your time. You want every student to see you doing what you said without showing any anger or frustration.
Furthermore, because no other teacher does this—after all, who in their right mind would hold someone accountable in the first few minutes—it says volumes about you and what you value.
Smile, do what you say, and they’ll respect and appreciate you right from the get-go.
x: The goal isn't the rule itself but the demonstration — showing new students, within the first few minutes, that the teacher does exactly what they say they'll do.

t: How to Handle A Bully Parent
q: A parent that demands, questions, browbeats, sabotages, and otherwise makes your life miserable can only be handled with a light but shrewd touch.
The idea is to be transparent from the get-go, get parents on record for understanding your program, and answer any and all potential complaints or reasons for dissatisfaction ahead of time.
The more they see you as a friend, the lower will be your status as an expert and master of your craft.

Say nothing until they’re finished, even if they mischaracterize you or make an assumption about an incident with their child. Most often, people who are angry just want to be heard. So hear them out.
Thus, if a parent approaches you, just smile and say “I wish I could help, but it’s not up to me. You might want to check with the office.
So always, always, always follow your classroom management plan as written and enforce it like an impartial referee .
When their weapons don’t work on you, they stop using them. They give up. They may pout, but they’ll no longer bother you.
